claims.text: Controlled thermal treatments can induce enhanced surface microsegregation in the target steels while leaving overall alloy composition constant.
Thermally induced surface microsegregation enriches chromium at the steel surface.
Surface chromium enrichment promotes formation of a stable chromium-rich passive film.
The chromium-rich passive film is the primary cause of superior corrosion resistance in these steels.
A chromium-rich passive film reduces interfacial charge transfer.
A chromium-rich passive film limits selective dissolution.
Higher local work function indicates a more noble local surface state associated with reduced anodic dissolution.
Differences in phase composition and work function can generate micro-galvanic cells and selective dissolution in duplex stainless steel.
Thermal treatments promoting surface microsegregation will produce greater surface chromium enrichment than standard processing.
Thermal treatments promoting surface microsegregation will produce higher local work functions than standard processing.
Thermal treatments promoting surface microsegregation will lower corrosion rates relative to uniformly processed controls.
Alloy chemistry affects selective reaction and surface depletion in aggressive chloride media.
The proposed mechanism applies across the pH, temperature, aggressive-species, and radiation ranges typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power service.
Conditions beyond the tested ranges may activate additional corrosion mechanisms.
Aggressive ions and associated impurities can alter corrosion reactions and complicate the observed response.
Identical alloys processed to have low and high surface microsegregation should be compared under identical corrosive environments.
Surface chromium, local work function, electrochemical corrosion rate, and mass loss are measurable study variables.
Failure to observe both increased chromium-rich film formation and decreased corrosion rate in the enhanced-microsegregation group is proposed as falsification.
